RESEARCH NOTE / T8

Comparative benchmarking of AI research agents for omics data interpretation

智能体技术与科研系统收录 2026-08-2010 分钟阅读
论文原文 ↗
  • Bibliographic status: Nikita V. Basov; Yosef K. Tirta; Zihan Li; Huan Zhou; Kiryl D. Piatkevich; 2026; 待核对; DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-10437888/v1
  • One-line takeaway: 论文定量比较三个已部署的生物医学科研智能体并讨论任务适配，属于当前稀缺的科学智能体横向基准；尽管领域是组学，其评价设计、能力边界和代理选择结论会直接影响CatMaster的对比实验与效用主张。

What the paper asks

AI research agents, which are claimed to accelerate or even replace human bioinformatics analysis, are being deployed rapidly in life sciences and biomedical research. However, many scientists lack a systematic approach to assessing their utility and to determining which agent is best suited to a given task. Here we quantitatively benchmark three biomedical AI research agents, including K-Dense (Gemini 2.5 Pro), Finch from Edison Scientific, and Biomni (Claude family), against ChatGPT, which our survey identified as the most commonly used approach for analysing omics datasets. For benchmarking, we performed bioinformatic analyses of metabolomic, bulk proteomic and bulk transcriptomic datasets, which are among the most frequently requested workflows submitted to the deployed AI agents. We evaluated all four agents using a process-anchored framework that scores each output on process quality, result reporting, and interpretation depth, while a domain-aware ordinal rubric is applied in parallel. Eight independent runs per agent per modality, together with bootstrap resampling, alternative scoring definitions, output-volume controls, and within-agent reproducibility measurements, quantified uncertainty. No single agent dominated across all modalities. K-Dense led in metabolomics with the most thorough, reproducible reports; Finch produced the best-organized reports and won proteomics and transcriptomics; Biomni offered the strongest biological interpretation but frequently omitted quality control and preprocessing; ChatGPT, without workflow scaffolding, managed only basic statistics and finished last.Furthermore, agent architecture, not base-model capability, dominates what each agent outputs, with processanchored evaluation reordering the field relative to accuracy alone. Our benchmark and rubric provide the community with an auditable basis for choosing among AI research agents for omics analysis.

We are currently witnessing a rapid acceleration in the generation of scientific data, particularly in the domains of proteomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics1,2,3. The rapid expansion of omics datasets creates a real bottleneck in data analysis and interpretation. Specifically, these datasets promote data-driven rather than hypothesis-driven research. In this mode, biological interpretation relies entirely on extracting new biological insights from the dataset itself, without preconceived hypotheses4.

In this context, bioinformaticians experience a bottleneck in analysing and interpreting the vast datasets. AI agents that can operate directly on large volumes of pre-processed omics data, e.g., expression tables, can significantly accelerate bioinformatic analysis, either assisting expert bioinformaticians or, in some cases, substituting for parts of the standard analysis workflow5,8. In the past two years, several AI agents specifically optimized for multi-omics data analysis have been introduced, including K-Dense9, Biomni7, and Finch (from Edison Scientific https://edisonscientific.com/). These agents allow scientists, even without a coding or bioinformatic background, to interact with their datasets and analyze them using standard bioinformatic workflows, and to generate new hypotheses to test, all through a user-friendly interface. Notably, our independent survey of practitioners revealed that many scientists in the field still rely on general-purpose ChatGPT LLMs to analyse omics data tables. Together, this rapid deployment creates a pressing need for careful benchmarking of these agents on standardized datasets6,10,30. Here, we perform a systematic benchmarking of the three biomedical agents (K-Dense, Biomni, Finch) against ChatGPT on three standard datasets in metabolomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics — the three most common data types submitted to such agents according to personal communication with Angela Yiu from Edison Scientific. Methods

Each agent output was converted into a fixed-dimensional feature representation using structural counts, methodological keyword dictionaries, biological keyword dictionaries and audit-oriented features. Structural features included document length, numbers of tables, code blocks, P-value mentions, false-discovery-rate or q-value mentions, fold-change mentions, gene-like tokens, dataset identifiers, figures, citations, units and numeric values. Methodological features captured terms related to quality control, normalisation, scaling, batch correction, imputation, statistical testing, multiple-testing correction, effect sizes, differential expression, alignment and quantification, principal component analysis, partial least squares discriminant analysis, volcano-plot and heatmap visualisation, and pathway enrichment. Biological features captured genes, transcripts, isoforms, proteins, metabolites, pathways, gene ontology, transcription factors, immune and inflammatory processes, cell cycle, apoptosis, metabolism, signalling, oxidative stress, biomarkers, non-coding RNA, splicing and epigenetic terms. Audit-oriented features captured preprocessing statements, significant-feature reporting, limitations, uncertainty, biological plausibility, annotation confidence, mechanistic interpretation and reproducibility language. Feature extraction was performed using case-insensitive regular-expression matching and curated keyword dictionaries. File-level feature vectors were concatenated into an 87-dimensional representation, summed to obtain run-level vectors and averaged across runs to obtain agent-level summaries. Keyword presence sets were also retained for Jaccard-based similarity analysis. The feature-extraction and aggregation procedures are described in Supplementary Methods, Section A, Algorithms 4–6.
